query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Multilayer high-entropy alloy (HEA) protective coatings with alternating compositions can achieve superior resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation because their engineered, mismatched, and potentially serrated interfaces act as effective dislocation barriers and modulate atomic diffusion, thereby reducing creep rates.
generation.material_initial_state: A multilayer HEA protective coating composed of alternating layers that have controlled differences in lattice parameters and/or precipitate content (e.g., varying γ and γ′ phase fractions) that are initially coherent or semi-coherent.
generation.intervention: Fabricate coatings with intentionally varied layer compositions and thicknesses to introduce periodic lattice misfits and interface morphology (e.g., engineered serrations) and then expose these coatings to elevated temperature, constant load conditions.
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions typical of protective coatings (e.g., 500–1000 °C) with applied stresses representative of service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The multilayer interfaces, through their controlled lattice misfits and possibly serrated morphologies, mediate local strain fields and act as pinning sites for dislocations, thus impeding their motion and hindering atomic diffusion across layers.
generation.mechanism: Inspired by reports that γ/γ′ interfaces and negatively mismatched interfaces in high-entropy superalloys block dislocation motion, the introduced heterointerfaces in the multilayer pattern impose additional barriers to dislocation glide and reduce effective diffusion paths. This results in higher activation energies for creep and a lower steady-state creep rate compared to monolithic HEA coatings.
generation.predicted_outcome: When compared with baseline homogeneous (monolithic) HEA coatings, the multilayer coatings will exhibit a significantly lower creep rate (e.g., a reduction on the order of 50–90% depending on multilayer parameters) and higher activation energy, along with microstructural evidence of dislocation pile-ups and less propagation across layers.
generation.baseline: Monolithic HEA coatings with uniform composition and microstructure, in which creep resistance is governed solely by the intrinsic properties of the alloy without engineered interfaces.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be effective under elevated temperature and moderate stress conditions where the individual layers retain their structural integrity and the interfaces remain stable. Excessively large misfits or incoherent interfaces, however, might lead to premature failure or interfacial decohesion.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on the interface-related creep resistance observed in HEA systems (as evidenced in PMC12842692 sections on γ/γ′ interface effects and lattice misfit effects) and extends it to engineered multilayer coatings (an aspect not directly examined by the provided evidence). The new element is the application of periodic compositional variations to create a network of dislocation-blocking interfaces in protective coatings, which must be validated experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of protective coatings: (a) multilayer HEA coatings with engineered alternating compositions and controlled interface morphology and (b) monolithic (uniform) HEA coatings. Subject both sets to accelerated creep testing at elevated temperatures (e.g., 600–800 °C) under the same constant stress. Perform high-resolution microstructural analysis (TEM, XRD) to assess dislocation pile-up and interface integrity.
measurements: Steady-state creep rate from strain–time curves
Activation energy for creep derived from temperature-dependent tests
Microstructural evaluation of dislocation density at and across interfaces
Assessment of interface morphology and lattice misfit via XRD and TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayer coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction in creep rate and an increase in activation energy (e.g., less than a 20% improvement) or if the microstructural analyses do not reveal evidence of enhanced dislocation blocking at the interfaces compared to the monolithic coating, then the hypothesis is falsified.
